title: Keeping Your Word: The Law of Vows
summary: Moses tells the tribal leaders that anyone who makes a vow to the LORD must keep it. The chapter then sets out when a woman's vow stands and when it may be cancelled: a father may annul the vow of a young daughter living at home, and a husband the vow of his wife, but only on the day he hears of it. A widow or divorced woman is bound by her own word.
story: The festival calendar of chapters 28 and 29 ended by mentioning vows and freewill offerings, which individuals brought in addition to the nation's public sacrifices (29:39). This chapter follows naturally, turning from the worship of the whole people to the promises individuals make to God. It continues the book's preparation of the new generation for life in the land, where households would be settled and where vows (to offer a sacrifice, to abstain from something, to dedicate a gift) would be part of ordinary piety. Earlier in Numbers, the Nazirite vow (chapter 6) and Israel's own vow before the battle at Hormah (21:2) show how seriously such promises were taken. The next chapter returns to the narrative with the war against Midian.
historical:
Vows were common across the ancient world. People promised gifts to their gods in exchange for help in sickness, danger, childlessness, or war, and inscriptions from Phoenician and other sites record offerings made in fulfillment of such vows. The Old Testament contains many examples. Jacob vowed at Bethel to give a tenth if God brought him home safely (Genesis 28:20-22). Hannah vowed that if God gave her a son she would give him to the LORD (1 Samuel 1:11), and her husband Elkanah allowed her vow to stand (1 Samuel 1:23). Jephthah's rash vow before battle (Judges 11) became a tragic example of a promise made carelessly. The wisdom writers warned against delaying to pay a vow and against rash words before God (Ecclesiastes 5:4-6; Proverbs 20:25).

The chapter is addressed to “the heads of the tribes” (verse 1), the leaders responsible for administering justice among their clans, since disputes over vows and household authority would come before them.
cultural:
Israel's households were organized around a male head, first the father and then, after marriage, the husband. He was responsible for the household's property and economic life, and a vow often involved property: an animal to be sacrificed, a gift to the sanctuary, or a period of abstaining from food or other things. A woman's vow could therefore commit resources that belonged to the household as a whole. The law protects both sides of this arrangement. It allows the head of the house to cancel a vow that would bind the household, but only promptly, on the day he hears of it, so that he cannot hold it over her later. If he stays silent, the vow stands. If he cancels it afterward, he bears the guilt himself (verse 15).

The law also protects the woman. If her father or husband cancels her vow, the LORD will absolve her; she is not guilty before God for failing to keep it. And a widow or divorced woman, who has no male head over her household, is treated as fully responsible for her own word (verse 9), just as a man is.
literary: The chapter is case law. It begins with a general principle for men (verse 2) and then works through a series of cases for women, each introduced with if: a young woman in her father's house (verses 3-5), a woman who marries while under a vow (verses 6-8), a widow or divorced woman (verse 9), and a married woman in her husband's house (verses 10-15). Each case has the same two branches: if he says nothing, the vow stands; if he forbids it on the day he hears, it does not, and the LORD will absolve her. The repetition makes the law easy to remember and apply. The closing verse (16) summarizes the chapter as statutes concerning a man and his wife, and a father and a daughter still at home.

outline.t: A man must keep every vow he makes
A young woman's vow in her father's house
A woman who marries while under a vow
A widow or divorced woman is bound by her word
A married woman's vow in her husband's house

doctrines.note: Vows are made “to the LORD”, and he takes words spoken to him seriously. The God who keeps every promise he makes expects his people to keep theirs.

The law assumes a household under a responsible head, and it limits that authority as well as granting it: a father or husband must act at once or not at all, and bears the guilt if he cancels a vow unfairly.
The chapter shows the law applying a basic principle (keep your word) to the real complications of family life, balancing the individual's commitment with the household's shared obligations.

words.note: Neder, vow. A vow was a promise to God, usually to give something or to do something, often made conditionally (if God does this, I will do that). Once spoken, it was binding. The word appears throughout the chapter and in the psalms, where worshipers speak of paying their vows in the assembly after God has answered.

Issar, a binding obligation or pledge. The word comes from a root meaning to bind or tie. It seems to describe a promise of abstinence, binding oneself to refrain from something. The chapter pairs it with neder, and its repeated language of binding (by which she has bound herself) shows how a spoken word before God was felt to tie the speaker.

Nu', to forbid or restrain. The same verb describes discouraging someone, and it is used in chapter 32 of the Reubenites and Gadites discouraging Israel from entering the land. Here it means a father or husband expressly forbidding a vow, which releases the woman from it.

christ: Jesus spoke directly to the practice of oaths and vows: “Again, you have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘Do not break your oath, but fulfill your vows to the Lord.’” He went further: “Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No’” (Matthew 5:33, 37). The law in Numbers insists that a word spoken to God must be kept; Jesus insists that every word should be so reliable that no special vow is needed to make it binding. Behind both stands the faithfulness of God himself. Paul says that all of God's promises find their Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). The God who swore oaths to Abraham kept them, and the New Testament presents Christ as the one in whom God's every promise is made good.

hard.q: Why can a father or husband cancel a woman's vow, but no one can cancel a man's?
hard.a: The chapter reflects the structure of an ancient Israelite household, where the father or husband was the legal and economic head. Because vows often committed property or affected the household's life, the head of the house was given the right to review them. Readers today rightly notice that the law does not treat men and women the same way. Interpreters respond in different ways. Some stress that the law assumes, rather than commands, the patriarchal structure of its time, and that the later biblical story moves toward a fuller expression of equal dignity (Galatians 3:28). Others read the law as setting out real responsibilities within the household that still carry meaning. Many point out that the chapter also limits male authority: the veto must be used at once, the woman is released from guilt if it is used, the man bears the guilt if he misuses it, and a woman who heads her own household is fully responsible for her word. Whatever one's conclusion, the law is less concerned with ranking men and women than with protecting the seriousness of words spoken to God.

questions: The chapter begins with a simple rule: do everything you have promised. Are there promises you have made, to God or to others, that you have quietly let slide?
A father or husband had to speak up on the day he heard of a vow or keep silent for good. What does that suggest about the timing and honesty of our responses to others?
Jesus taught that our yes should simply mean yes. How would your speech change if every word carried the weight of a vow?
